message.content: Semiconductor prices are moving in more than one direction at this point in the cycle, with the cost of compute falling while prices are bid up in the parts of the supply chain where capacity is tightest [D7]. The cost of the graphical processing units used to train and run AI models has declined precipitously, continuing a longer trend of algorithmic and hardware efficiency gains [D7]. High-bandwidth memory, by contrast, has become a binding constraint as models scale, and the Korean export price indexes for DRAM and semiconductors serve as a proxy for these input costs [D7]. Mature-node shortages are the other source of upward pressure and are expected to persist, which turns supply chain management into a pricing lever, while prices for some processors are separately reported to be rising again [D3]. Three things are driving or capping these prices. The first is AI-related demand, since rising semiconductor production alongside capital expenditure is the indicator that supply is expanding to meet AI-driven demand, consistent with continued cost relief in compute terms [D7]. The second is upstream concentration, because the intermediate processing and refining stages for the materials that batteries, magnets and semiconductors require remain highly concentrated, and ultra-high-purity gallium refining and compound semiconductor manufacturing rely on only one or two specialised equipment suppliers [D4]. The third is the build-out of Chinese manufacturing capacity across mature-node chips, memory and packaging, which adds supply and works against higher prices [D8]. On the capping side, critical minerals account for a small share of downstream product prices, so downstream users may be able to absorb higher material costs without materially affecting end-product prices, which provides scope for diversified sourcing [D4]. Export controls targeting not only critical minerals but also processing technologies and equipment nonetheless tighten the availability of inputs the industry depends on, and closing those capability gaps is framed as a requirement for diversified supply chains [D4]. Government programmes aimed at advancing the commercial readiness of mineral processing technologies list semiconductors among their target applications [D9]. The industry's own reported shipments and orders are not adjusted for price changes, so those series cannot separate price from volume on their own [D1][D6]. New orders and unfilled orders in the durable goods report exclude semiconductor manufacturing data altogether [D6]. Overall manufacturing capacity utilization remains below its long-run average, leaving room for output to expand [D2]. The industry is nevertheless expected to grow strongly, with the growth of the AI chip market and geopolitical competition between the United States and China shaping how it develops [D5].
